A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 4.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (BR), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 34.5 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (CN), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 33.1 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (ID), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.5 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (ES), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (IT), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 52.5 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (KR), medium harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 1.9 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (CA), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 10.6 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (MX), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (TR), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 10.2 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (TH), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.2 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (UA), large harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (FI), medium harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 6.3 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (RU), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 63.4 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (PF), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 52.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (JP), medium harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 5.6 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (NZ), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (GR), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (MY), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (HR), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (QA), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (IT), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 6.3 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (RU), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (IT), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 52.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (JP), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 83.6 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (CO), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 4.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (BR), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 52.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (JP), large harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (SE), medium harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.0 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (LC), small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.

A measurable share of the fishing vessels calling here were flagged high-risk by the published behavioural model (McDonald et al., PNAS 2021), which is trained on 27 observable vessel behaviours — among them AIS gaps over 12 and over 24 hours, presence on an official IUU fishing list, flag of convenience, visits to ports of convenience, and transhipment events with IUU or known forced-labour vessels. A model output, and a disputed one: a reply in the same journal notes that only 21 of 193 known abuse vessels produced profiles the method could use, and that the features are not causally linked to conditions on board. Treat it as where the model is pointing, not as what is there. 0.8 (country-level: this applies to the port state, not to this port specifically) Port listed in the World Port Index (US), very small harbour. Ports are on this map because the port state is where the inspection powers sit: ILO Convention 188 and the Maritime Labour Convention give it authority to inspect and give a fisher or seafarer an onshore complaint route, and the FAO Port State Measures Agreement is built on the port being the chokepoint. Long voyages without port calls and repeated transhipment at sea are documented forced-labour indicators — see the ILO indicator framework and Global Fishing Watch's published risk modelling. The customs classification above is not one of those indicators: it describes what the port is for trade purposes, and no one has validated it as a labour signal. Note that this marks where the mechanism operates and is not evidence that anyone here is necessarily exploited.
